certainty_reasoning: The sexual reading, standard across major biographers, rests on later Ross statements reported in secondary literature not yet read in the source for this project (Ellmann/McKenna verification is a standing next step). The suppressed dedication, added: Wilde composed a dedication to Ross for The Ballad - 'When I came out of prison / some met me with garments and with spices, / and others with wise counsel. / You met me with love' - deliberately without initials or name, and it was never printed (editors' note, printed 973).
date_label: Met 1886 (Ross: 'I only met him in '86'); Ross dated the intimacy to the Lady Windermere period, c. 1891; regular correspondence only after the downfall; to Wilde's death, 30 Nov. 1900, with Ross at the bedside; literary executor thereafter.
summary: Ross met Wilde in 1886 and remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. The surviving correspondence opens in October 1888 ('My dear Bobbie … I shall miss you in town') and by 1889 runs to 'Yours, with much love'; Ross himself dated their intimacy to the period when Wilde was writing Lady Windermere (c. 1891). After 1895 Ross became the relationship's practical center - regular correspondent, supervisor of the De Profundis typescript at his Hornton Street lodgings, daily attendant of the final illness who fetched the priest for Wilde's deathbed reception into the Catholic Church - and he was holding Wilde's hand at the death on 30 November 1900. He buried Wilde at Bagneux in a concession hired in his own name, moved the remains to Père Lachaise in 1909, and administered the literary estate.

sources.quote: No other friend have I now in this beautiful world. I want no other. … My poem should have run, 'When I came out of prison you met me with garments, with spices, with wise counsel. You met me with love.' Not others did it, but you.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [28 May 1897], Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer - his first days out of prison, alone for the first time. Editors' n. 2 gives the lines in their verse form and records that they were intended as a second dedication to The Ballad of Reading Gaol and removed at proof stage.
sources.supports: Wilde naming what Ross was to him, in his own words: the one friend left to him, and the one who met him at his release with love rather than counsel - the most explicit first-hand characterization of the bond in the correspondence read
sources.provenance: PDF pages 908-909, printed folios 858 and 859 confirmed on the rendered pages. The quoted run spans the page-turn; the elision drops the passage on Wilde fearing he harms Ross, the naming of him as St Robert of Phillimore, and the sentence introducing the misquoted lines. 'you' is italicised in the printed text of the poem lines.

sources.quote: Robert Baldwin Ross (1869–1918) was a Canadian. … He first met Wilde in 1886 and remained his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, biographical footnote on Ross, hung on Wilde's first surviving letter to him (c. 13 October 1888); the note asserts friendship and executorship only, no sexual claim
sources.supports: Frame of the bond: met 1886; 'most faithful friend' to Wilde's death; literary executor
sources.provenance: PDF page 382, printed folio 360 confirmed on rendered page. Genealogical detail between the two quoted sentences elided.

sources.quote: And oh! Bobbie, let us have an evening together. What ages since we had a talk! Yours, with much love OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Ross, [Late July 1889], from Kreuznach; close of the letter, valediction and signature as printed
sources.supports: Warmest register of the early correspondence: 'Yours, with much love' (1889)
sources.provenance: PDF page 431, printed folio 409 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: But I only met him in '86 and only became intimate with him when he was writing Lady Windermere, but there were long intervals when I never saw him, and he never corresponded with me regularly until after the downfall.
sources.context: Ross to Adela Schuster, 14 December 1900, printed in the Epilogue; 'Lady Windermere' italicized in the original; Ross declining the suggestion that he become Wilde's Boswell
sources.supports: Ross's own timeline: met Wilde 1886, intimacy only from the Lady Windermere period (c. 1891) - complicates the common claim that the liaison began in 1886
sources.provenance: PDF page 1274, printed folio 1229 confirmed on rendered page; key sentences re-verified on 4x zoomed region render.
sources.speaker: Robert Ross

sources.quote: I went to the bedside and held his hand, his pulse began to flutter. He heaved a deep sigh, the only natural one I had heard since I arrived, the limbs seemed to stretch involuntarily, the breathing came fainter; he passed at 10 minutes to 2 p.m. exactly.
sources.context: Ross to More Adey, 14 December 1900, narrating Wilde's death at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, on 30 November 1900; Ross and Reggie Turner were the two friends present
sources.supports: Ross at the bedside holding Wilde's hand at the moment of death - the terminal point of the lifelong bond
sources.provenance: PDF page 1265, printed folio 1220 confirmed on rendered page.
sources.speaker: Robert Ross

sources.quote: Little did Eliza Ross or Constance Wilde suspect, when they finalized this arrangement, that some time the previous year, the thirty-two-year-old Oscar and the seventeen-year-old Robbie had become lovers.
sources.context: Fryer introducing Ross's 1887 residence as the Wildes' lodger at 16 Tite Street, Chelsea. The biographer's own assertion, not a participant's words. Ages stated exactly as Fryer states them (readme register rule).
sources.supports: Ross's dedicated biographer dates the start of a sexual relationship to 1886 - the traditional dating, against which Ross's own 1900 letter to Adela Schuster stands.
sources.provenance: PDF page 32 of Fryer_2000_Robbie-Ross, printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page. Note the offset is not constant in this scan (+14 here, +22 after the plate section).

sources.quote: Whatever the precise circumstances of the contact being forged, it would appear that young Robbie seduced Oscar some time in 1886, and that this was Oscar's first experience of a homosexual act. Oscar told his friend, the journalist and wit Reggie Turner, that this was the case. Robbie himself later confirmed it to one of Wilde's earliest biographers, Arthur Ransome.
sources.context: Same page, after Fryer dismisses Frank Harris's public-lavatory story of the first meeting. Fryer gives no note for these sentences; neither Wilde's remark to Turner nor Ross's confirmation to Ransome is quoted or sourced on the page.
sources.supports: A reported chain of participant testimony for the 1886 dating - Wilde told Turner, Ross told Ransome - which is the nearest thing Fryer offers to first-person evidence. It remains Fryer's report of an unsourced oral confirmation, not the participant's surviving words: a lead toward self-reported evidence rather than an instance of it.
sources.provenance: PDF page 32, printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page. Contiguous sentences; the preceding block on the same page is quoted separately, with no elision joining them.

sources.quote: It should not be assumed, however, that Oscar and Robbie conducted a passionate, clandestine affair on the premises. On the contrary, it is unlikely that they did, and not only for reasons of propriety. Despite the initial seduction, and the huge bond of affection between them, neither was physically each other's 'type'.
sources.context: Fryer on the months of 1887 when Ross lodged at Tite Street. He continues that Ross 'was far more interested sexually in youths of his own age than in the rather portly, flabby, albeit fascinating Oscar Wilde.'
sources.supports: Fryer separates a single initiating episode in 1886 from a sustained affair, and denies the latter for 1887 - supplying the middle term under which the 1886 tradition and Ross's own 'only became intimate. Lady Windermere' (1900) can both be true. Fryer never cites the Schuster letter, so the reconciliation is available from him but not stated by him.
sources.provenance: PDF page 35, printed folio 21 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: In fact, Robbie was already, at the age of nineteen, much more than a disciple and sometime lover for Oscar. The two could talk frankly, despite the difference in their ages, and bounce ideas off each other.
sources.context: Fryer at the turn of 1888-89, Ross's first year at King's College, Cambridge. Age stated exactly as Fryer states it.
sources.supports: Fryer's summary formula for the bond - 'disciple and sometime lover'. 'Sometime' is his word, and his second signal that he does not read the relationship as a continuous affair.
sources.provenance: PDF page 47, printed folio 33 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Robbie seems to have felt no jealousy towards John Gray. Indeed, he was remarkably generous and understanding when it came to Oscar's other lovers. Of course, he himself was enjoying various encounters with youths, though none at this stage held any claim to his affections, let alone to the sort of love he felt for Oscar.
sources.context: C. 1889-90, immediately before the family council that sent Ross to Edinburgh away from 'myriad temptations, including Oscar Wilde'. Fryer's own characterisation of Ross's feeling; no participant statement is quoted.
sources.supports: The asymmetry Fryer builds the life on: Ross in love with Wilde and unpossessive about Gray and Wilde's other lovers, while sexually occupied elsewhere. Bears on the ross--wilde bond and on why no jealousy edge to gray or douglas is warranted.
sources.provenance: PDF page 56, printed folio 42 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: As for dear Robbie, if he will kindly send me out a pair of his oldest boots I will blacken them with pleasure, and send them back to him with a sonnet. I have loved Robbie all my life, and have not the smallest intention of giving up loving him. Of all my old friends he is the one who has the most beautiful nature; had my other friends been like him, I would not be the pariah-dog of the nineteenth century. But natures like his are not found twice in a life-time. When dear Robbie heavily bombarded me (an unfair thing, as unfortified places are usually respected in civilised war) I bore it with patriarchal patience. I admit, however, that when he seemed to me slightly casual about someone else, I sent up a rocket of several colours. I am sorry I did so.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Saturday [11 December 1897], Villa Giudice, Posilippo (MS Hyde) - written to a third party, which is what makes it worth having. Wilde is living with Douglas at posilippo as he writes it, and Ross had been 'bombarding' him with objections to that. He is not appeasing Ross here and he is not writing to him; he is telling his publisher what he thinks, in a letter Ross was never meant to see. The quarrel he apologises for is over Ross being 'slightly casual about someone else' - the someone else is not named on the page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The plainest statement of the Ross attachment anywhere in the correspondence, made behind Ross's back and therefore not flattery.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1054; printed folio 1006 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I am at the Roma, the first time for ten days. Would you were here. Do you observe that I have fallen in love with you again? Our Indian winter. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Rome, April 1900 - the close of the letter, quoted whole. It comes directly after the paragraph describing Armando's body, on the same folio, which is the reason to have both: Wilde tells Ross he has fallen in love with him again in the sentence after describing another young man's thighs. Seven months before his death. 'Our Indian winter' is a late warm spell. during the General Index sweep, from a folio reached by following an index entry for Armando - not by reading the Ross correspondence, which remains largely unread.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde telling Ross he had fallen in love with him again, in his last year.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1230; printed folio 1184 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I also go to look at that beautiful voluptuous marble boy I went to worship with you at the Museo Nazionale. What a lovely thing it is!
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Rome, April 1900. A shared act of looking, recalled: the two of them had gone together to worship a statue. From the reading log, which recorded it as read-but-unlogged on the folio taken for Armando.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Something the two of them had done together, and the word Wilde used for it.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1228; printed folio 1182 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: This is a really lovely little place: only reached by mules or boats. … Have not yet been here: but have decided to enter the chiostro - just the place for me.
sources.context: Two postcards from Wilde to Robert Ross, both postmarked 7 April 1899, the first from Portofino and the second from San Fruttuoso (MS Clark), quoted whole and joined by an ellipsis. Both are signed 'S. M.' - Sebastian Melmoth. 'chiostro' the editors gloss as cloister. : read at the page and left unlogged. Trivial in content and kept for what it shows - that Wilde sent Ross postcards from wherever he was, twice in a day.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ordinary daily traffic of the friendship.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1187; printed folio 1141 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I am going to have a dedication. I don't put any initials or name. I simply say: When I came out of prison / some met me with garments and with spices, / and others with wise counsel. / You met me with love. Please let me see it in some nice type. I think it a beautiful and simple dedication. I hope you do too.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [October 1897], Villa Giudice, Posillipo - quoted whole from where the dedication is raised. The dedication is to Ross and it was never printed. The editors' footnote is unambiguous: 'These words were addressed to Robbie Ross, but they did not appear in The Ballad.' Wilde is explicit that the name is to be withheld - 'I don't put any initials or name' - so what he proposed was an unsigned declaration that only its addressee would recognise, and even that was dropped. A second, published dedication went instead to C. T. W., the hanged trooper. Note also the setting: Wilde was at Posillipo living with Douglas as he wrote this. Corrected - an earlier note of mine filed this phrase as Wilde writing to Smithers about Smithers, because the line sits in a letter to Smithers and the page-break hid the footnote. Re-reading the following folio settled it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A dedication of love to Ross, composed, shown to the publisher, and then suppressed.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1021; printed folio 973 confirmed on the rendered page image.
